overview: TradeWindow is a small-cap NZX-listed (and, since December 2025, ASX Foreign Exempt-listed) global trade software company selling digital tools for exporters, importers, freight forwarders and customs brokers across New Zealand, Australia and, to a lesser extent, other Asia-Pacific markets. Its modular platform (Prodoc, Origin, Cube, Tariff, Freight/SpeEDI) digitises trade documents, certificates of origin, customs/tariff classification and freight-forwarding workflows, and the company is now investing heavily in a next-generation 'Freight AI' operating system. TradeWindow has been loss-making every year since its 2021 listing, funding growth and product development through repeated dilutive capital raises rather than internally generated cash.

business_model.summary: SaaS/subscription model layered with per-transaction fees: customers pay recurring subscription fees per module/user (Freight, Cube) plus on-demand transaction fees for document creation/sharing (Origin, e-commerce), and one-off installation/service fees. ~94% of trading revenue is recurring in nature (subscription + repeat transactional). Revenue is disaggregated as roughly 53% transactional, 41% subscription, 3% installation, 3% service (FY25 mix). The company discloses ARR (running ahead of trading revenue as new customers/modules ramp), Active Customers, ARPC for Shippers and for Freight Forwarders, and a Customer Retention Rate as its core KPIs.
business_model.customer_type: B2B - exporters, importers, freight forwarders and customs brokers, ranging from mid-market to large enterprise; low concentration (no single customer >6% of trading revenue per FY25 annual report)
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand and Australia are the core markets, with Australia now over 50% of the customer base and the primary growth driver; small presence in the wider Asia-Pacific/rest of world. Operations/staff also based in the Philippines, Singapore, Indonesia and the USA.

main_competitors: legacy/in-house freight-forwarder systems and manual/paper-based processes
competitive_position.market_position: Sub-scale niche challenger in a market dominated by WiseTech Global, a multi-billion-dollar incumbent; TradeWindow explicitly frames its strategy as targeting WiseTech's mid-market customers with a lower-cost, AI-first alternative. FY25 trading revenue of ~NZ$8.0m and FY26 of ~NZ$9.6m is immaterial next to WiseTech's >A$1bn revenue base.

moat_factors.description: Multi-module adoption (Prodoc, Origin, Cube, Freight, Tariff) and integration into customer/border-agency workflows creates some stickiness, evidenced by rising ARPC as customers add modules, but the company's own retention rate has been volatile (97% H1 FY25 to 87% FY25 to 89% FY26) and 2H FY25 saw retention deliberately traded off to prune low-value accounts.

TradeWindow is officially authorised by NZ Customs Service and Australian DFAT to issue Certificates of Origin, and connects directly with border agencies via EDI - a real but narrow and geographically limited barrier to entry.
Minimal brand recognition outside Australasia and no scale advantage versus WiseTech or E2open; company is explicitly the smaller, capital-constrained challenger.

Cube's blockchain-based multi-party collaboration and the planned Freight AI platform could create some network value across shippers/forwarders/carriers/customs, but this is aspirational rather than proven at TradeWindow's current scale.

weaknesses: Sub-scale relative to WiseTech Global and E2open, both far better capitalised for AI/product investment
High customer churn/rationalisation history (retention swung from 97% to 87% within a single year)
Revenue base still small (~NZ$8-10m) making unit economics and fixed-cost leverage fragile
Heavy reliance on continued equity funding rather than organic cash generation to fund product roadmap

growth_drivers: Freight AI - next-generation AI-enabled freight operating system targeting automation and decision support for mid-market freight forwarders; first e-commerce module targeted before end of FY26, full platform targeted for rollout around September 2027
Australian market penetration - >50% of customers now Australian; continued cross-sell of Cube, Origin, Tariff modules into that base
ARR growth outpacing trading revenue (ARR $8.7m FY25 -> $8.8m 1H FY26 -> $10.1m FY26, surpassing $10m for the first time) as new large enterprise customers and price increases fully annualise
ARPC expansion - shipper and freight-forwarder average revenue per customer both growing 20%+ per period as customers adopt more modules
ASX Foreign Exempt Listing (completed 19 December 2025) intended to broaden the investor base and access to Australian institutional capital
Partnership-led distribution (e.g., IFCBAA partnership driving Tariff subscriptions among Australian freight forwarders) to extend reach without heavy incremental sales cost
Structural tailwind from increasing trade-regulation complexity, e-commerce growth and supply-chain visibility needs cited by management as durable demand drivers

business.description: FY2025 audited accounts carried explicit 'material uncertainty' going-concern language, with cash of only $0.4m against a $1.0m ASB loan; the company was reliant on hitting a tightly-scoped monthly EBITDA breakeven and stress-tested forecasts. Cash position has since improved materially (NZ$4.2m and no bank debt at FY26 year-end, aided by ASX-related capital raises), but the company's short operating history includes repeated near-term liquidity stress and its FY26 auditor opinion should be checked for whether the going-concern qualification was lifted.

Retention swung from 97% (H1 FY25) to 87% (FY25) to 89% (FY26) as management deliberately pruned lower-value accounts; total customer count has been flat-to-declining (554 -> 534 -> 547) even as ARPC rises, indicating growth is now concentrated in fewer, larger accounts.

EBITDA breakeven guidance has slipped from monthly breakeven achieved in March 2025 to an annual FY26 target, and has now been pushed out again to FY27 in order to fund accelerated Freight AI development - a pattern of moving goalposts that increases execution risk.

business.risk: Competitive/technology risk from Freight AI bet
business.description: Company is explicitly prioritising a multi-year AI platform investment (rollout targeted ~September 2027) over near-term profitability; if Freight AI fails to differentiate against WiseTech/E2open or is delayed further, the company will have sacrificed profitability for an unrealised product.

financial.description: History of repeated capital raises since the 2021 IPO: $6.8m convertible note conversion at listing, $14.7m raise (FY2023) that itself fell well short of a $20m target (only 27% raised, ~$5.4m), $600k placement (June 2025), $2.0-2.2m raise (FY2025), and an ~NZ$5.8m (A$5m) placement settled 15 December 2025 alongside the ASX listing, plus a further ~NZ$5.9m raise/SPP completed February 2026. Shareholders have been repeatedly diluted and should expect this to continue while the company remains loss-making.

financial.risk: Small absolute cash buffer versus cash-burn history
financial.description: Despite the improved NZ$4.2m FY26 cash balance, TradeWindow's monthly cash burn has historically run at material levels relative to its balance sheet (as high as ~$1m/month at points in its history); any slippage in the FY27 breakeven target would erode the buffer quickly.
AUD/NZD cross-currency exposure from Australian revenue growth and the AUD-denominated placement; ASX-quoted shares add a second currency/venue to manage.

regulatory.description: Certificate-of-origin issuance authority from NZ Customs and Australian DFAT is core to the Origin product; loss or narrowing of this accreditation, or new competing government digital-trade initiatives, could impair a key customer-acquisition channel.

Company handles sensitive trade, customs and financial data across multiple jurisdictions (NZ, Australia, and support operations in the Philippines, Singapore, Indonesia, USA); the FY25 annual report explicitly lists cybersecurity as a monitored material risk.

macro.description: Revenue is more sensitive to volume of trade than value, per management; the FY25/26 outlook commentary flags increased US tariffs and general trade-policy volatility as risks that could slow exports from key customer markets (agriculture, meat, seafood, horticulture, dairy) even though management argues NZ/Australia's web of free-trade agreements partly mitigates this.

As an early-stage, loss-making tech company reliant on external capital, TWL's ability to raise equity is sensitive to broader risk appetite for small-cap growth/AI tech names; the 2023 raise falling well short of target illustrates this vulnerability in a tighter funding environment.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global trade-tech/TradeTech software market is growing, driven by digitisation of customs and freight-forwarding processes, e-commerce cross-border growth, and increasing regulatory complexity (tariffs, rules of origin, sanctions); TradeWindow cites a US$2.8 trillion addressable TradeTech market opportunity, though this is an industry-level figure, not a company-specific serviceable market estimate.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - revenue correlates with trade volumes (exports/imports, e-commerce shipment activity) and is seasonal (management notes stronger H2 due to agricultural export peak season and Black Friday/Christmas retail volumes), rather than being purely subscription-smooth.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Indirect but meaningful - as an unprofitable micro-cap dependent on equity capital markets, higher rates/tighter risk appetite raise the cost and availability of the funding TWL needs before it reaches self-sustaining cash generation.
key_input_costs: Software engineering/AI development talent (R&D and Commercialisation ~36% of FY25 expenses)
Sales and partnership costs in Australia

recent_developments.event: FY26 full-year results: trading revenue up 20% to NZ$9.6m, ARR surpassed NZ$10m for the first time (NZ$10.1m), EBITDA loss narrowed to NZ$1.2m, net loss after tax NZ$2.6m, gross margin 60% (63% in Q4). Cash balance NZ$4.2m with no bank debt. Customer base 547 (down 7), retention improved to 89%. FreightAI development costs of NZ$661k capitalised to 31 March 2026, with NZ$1.5m more budgeted for FY27; full platform targeted for ~September 2027 rollout. FY27 guidance: 13-18% trading revenue growth with EBITDA approaching breakeven.
Share Purchase Plan closed, raising ~NZ$217k (866,962 shares), completing an approximately NZ$5.9m capital raise alongside the earlier placement.
TradeWindow completed its Foreign Exempt Listing on the ASX under ticker TWL, aiming to broaden its investor base into Australian institutional capital.

Settlement of the ~A$5m (~NZ$5.8m) conditional placement to Australian and New Zealand wholesale/institutional investors at A$0.22/NZ$0.25 per share, used to fund Freight AI acceleration, strengthen the balance sheet (including debt repayment) and support the ASX listing.

1H FY26 results: trading revenue up 25% to NZ$4.6m, ARR up 21% to NZ$8.8m, ARPC up ~20% for both shippers ($2,484/mo) and freight forwarders ($1,097/mo), retention improved to 92%. EBITDA loss narrowed to $0.65m; net loss after tax narrowed to $1.3m. Company disclosed that it deferred its previously guided FY26 annual EBITDA breakeven to FY27 to accelerate Freight AI investment in response to competitive pressure and customer demand.

FY2025 annual report (year ended 31 March 2025) disclosed explicit going-concern 'material uncertainty' language, cash of NZ$0.4m against a NZ$1.0m ASB Bank loan (guaranteed, with covenants), and reported that the company achieved its first monthly EBITDA breakeven in March 2025 after a 77% narrowing of the annual EBITDA loss to NZ$1.5m.

items.notes: Down from the 20% growth delivered in FY26 and well below the 25-37.5% range originally guided for FY26; management frames this as prudent given macro/trade-disruption uncertainty.

Annual EBITDA breakeven target was originally FY26, then pushed to FY27 (announced Nov 2025) to fund accelerated Freight AI investment; FY27 language is 'approaching' breakeven, not a firm breakeven commitment, which itself may signal a further soft slip.
Follows NZ$661k capitalised internal development cost to 31 March 2026; full platform rollout targeted around September 2027.
Materially improved from NZ$0.4m cash and a NZ$1.0m ASB loan at 31 March 2025, following the December 2025 ASX-linked placement and February 2026 SPP.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO AJ Smith, Chair Alasdair MacLeod) has consistently framed the strategy as prioritising growth and Freight AI investment over near-term profitability, arguing this builds long-term leadership in AI-enabled trade technology. The FY27 guidance explicitly acknowledges macroeconomic uncertainty and potential trade disruption as reasons for a more moderate growth rate and only 'approaching' (not achieving) EBITDA breakeven.

bull_case: ARR has crossed NZ$10m for the first time and continues to grow faster than trading revenue, with ARPC for both shipper and freight-forwarder segments compounding at 20%+ per period as customers adopt more modules

Balance sheet has been meaningfully de-risked over the past year: cash improved from NZ$0.4m (with a NZ$1.0m bank loan) at FY25 to NZ$4.2m with no bank debt at FY26, reducing near-term going-concern pressure
Gross margin trending higher (60% FY26, 63% in Q4) as the TW Freight cloud migration completes, providing operating leverage as revenue scales

ASX Foreign Exempt Listing broadens the investor base and capital-raising options beyond the thin NZX micro-cap market, and the company has now completed two raises post-listing without a shortfall like 2023's

Freight AI targets a genuine gap versus larger, technology-debt-laden incumbents (WiseTech, E2open) in the underserved mid-market freight-forwarder segment, and low customer concentration (no customer >6% of revenue) reduces single-customer risk
bear_case: Six consecutive years of losses and a demonstrated pattern of pushing out profitability targets (monthly breakeven March 2025 -> annual FY26 -> annual FY27 'approaching' breakeven) suggest management's forecasts should be treated with caution

FY2025 audited accounts carried an explicit going-concern 'material uncertainty' qualification; even with an improved FY26 cash balance, the company's short history includes a near-miss on liquidity and a 2023 capital raise that reached only 27% of its target, showing funding is not guaranteed to be available on demand

Extensive and repeated shareholder dilution (2021 note conversion, 2023 ~$5.4m raise, FY2025 ~$2.2m raise, Dec-2025 ~NZ$5.8m placement, Feb-2026 ~NZ$5.9m SPP) has diluted existing holders multiple times and is likely to continue while the company remains loss-making and investing in Freight AI

Customer retention has been volatile (97% to 87% to 89% across recent periods) and total customer counts have declined even as ARPC rises, meaning growth is increasingly dependent on a narrower set of larger accounts

TradeWindow is a sub-scale challenger (~NZ$9.6m FY26 revenue) competing against WiseTech Global, a multibillion-dollar incumbent with vastly greater resources to invest in AI and product development, raising real doubt about TradeWindow's ability to win and hold share over the multi-year Freight AI investment horizon
